findings.detail: D2 [verdict guardrails (b), (f) and the freeze sentence; CL17; practicalImplications[4]] Two new pilot parameters conflict. The pilot is 'at most 90 days', yet 'any missed deadline freezes the pilot at its current size'. The 90-day deliverable (f), an independent test of the new surfaces, falls on the pilot's last day. The draft never says what happens if (f) slips: does the pilot end, or does it continue frozen with no end date? A frozen pilot with no end date is the 'pilot quietly becomes permanent' failure that tradeoffs[1] warns about. There is a smaller ambiguity too. 'No admins' presumably means no privileged end users, but the tenant still needs our own IAM administrators, and their accounts would be exposed to the admin-console surface (BW-07). The draft does not say how those accounts are handled.

D1 [verdict (pilot guardrails, last sentences); alternatives 'Staged or limited rollout (pilot) with guardrails'; practicalImplications[4]; CL17] The pilot guardrails added in draft 2 do not cover the outcome most likely to matter: confirmation that the known Highs are still open. Rollback fires only on 'any new open High or Critical finding', and a freeze happens only on a 'missed deadline'. Suppose the 30-day retest or closure evidence (guardrail e) arrives on time and shows BW-04 (session survives password reset) or BW-07 (admin export IDOR) is still open, or that BW-11 has no rate limiting. Then neither trigger fires, because the findings are not new and the deadline was met. The pilot would keep running with confirmed account-takeover persistence and a directory-exposure flaw. The draft's own unlock criteria require closure of BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11, so the guardrails should match: rollback or suspension when delivered evidence confirms any of them is still open, not only when a new finding appears. Excluding admins from the pilot does not neutralise BW-07, because the draft itself (edgeCases[1]) says a lower-privilege session may be able to exploit it.

D3 [tradeoffs[0]; CL16] tradeoffs[0] says DBIR reports 'password-based access' as the top breach vector. E22 actually says 'compromised or stolen credentials' were the top initial access vector, at 22%. The draft also uses the 22% figure without restating E22's own caveat that it comes only from a snippet, because the Verizon report was not inspected. The DBIR comparison would read better with that caveat.

openDecisiveGaps: Can Keystone ID disable the Device Authorization Grant per tenant, enforce phishing-resistant or passkey-only MFA, restrict admin export, scope SCIM tokens, run SSO without SCIM, and stream admin and provisioning audit events to a SIEM?

Is there independent evidence (a retest letter or our own tenant test) that BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11 are closed on the current session service, and is there a SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 attestation whose scope covers provisioner-v2, the device grant and passkeys?
What does the organisation use today for workforce authentication and provisioning (incumbent IdP, MFA coverage, deprovisioning latency, fallback path if a pilot is rolled back)?
Does the full signed Brightwater report, obtained directly from Brightwater, match the vendor-supplied summary (scope, finding IDs, severities, statuses)?
Will the vendor permit a customer-commissioned penetration test of our tenant, and will it agree contractually to retest rights, breach-notification and availability SLAs, and data residency terms?
